newsitem.title: USA: Whitewater prosector to remain on Clinton probe.
newsitem.headline: Whitewater prosector to remain on Clinton probe.

text.p: Whitewater prosecutor Kenneth Starr admitted on Friday he had made a major mistake and reversed his decision to leave the investigation involving President Bill Clinton and his wife, vowing to stay for any major prosecutions.

Bowing to nearly a week of public criticism even from his own staff over his plan to move to a new career at Pepperdine University this summer, Starr abruptly changed his mind and said he was putting that plan on hold indefinitely.

At a news conference, he admitted his decision to leave was "unwise" and "incorrect" and "imprudent" -- it drew some strong editorial criticism, while delighting White House aides -- and had shaken public confidence in the investigation.
Quoting a famous line from a onetime New York City Mayor Fiorello LaGuardia, who was known for the pithy phrase, Starr said with a smile: "When I make a mistake, it's a 'beaut'."

In his formal statement, which he read, Starr said: "I have informed Pepperdine University ... that I do intend to continue as independent counsel, and that I will assume no duties or responsibilities at Pepperdine until the investigation and any resulting prosecutions of persons named in the order appointing me as independent counsel or high-ranking government officials have been substantially completed ..."
"My commitment is to the American people and to the pursuit of the truth, and I will seek to fulfil that commitment to the best of my ability and for as long as it takes," Starr said.

He noted the "persons named in the order" appointing him were President Clinton, Hillary Rodham Clinton and James McDougal, their business partner in the Whitewater land deal and head of a failed Arkansas Savings and Loan.
McDougal has been convicted on bank fraud charges and Starr said he was now talking with Whitewater investigators who are trying to persuade him to become a witness.
Beyond that, however, Starr refused to say anything about the state or direction of his investigation, whether he anticipated indictments, or how long it might take.

Starr's inquiry started in 1994 as a probe of the Whitewater land deal involving the Clintons when the president was governor of Arkansas as well as the failure of an Arkansas savings and loan institution run by McDougal.
It has since expanded to include a number of White House controversies including the firing of the travel office staff and the obtaining of FBI personal files.

Pepperdine University, located in Malibu, California, announced on Monday that Starr had accepted the appointment to become dean of its law school and was expected to leave the special prosecutor post for his new duties by August.

His decision to walk away from the highest-profile investigative job in the country, and one possibly involving the fate of the president and his wife, created a sensation -- and Washington was soon awash in speculation as to what it meant.

The conclusion of many legal experts and political analysts -- despite Starr's protestations -- was that he was leaving because he did not have enough evidence to prosecute the Clintons. The conclusion was that they must be home free.
In trying to counter that guesswork, Starr initially insisted his move meant nothing more than that he was accepting a fine career opportunity and a stroke of good fortune for himself and his family.

White House aides could barely conceal their glee at his initial decision to leave. Clinton had long ago endorsed the view that Starr, a Republican, was running a politically inspired investigation. The president is a Democrat.
The White House staff mood darkened when Friday's news of Starr's reversal broke. They declined any comment beyond personal puzzlement at his on-again, off-again moves.
Starr declined to predict whether he still might be able to leave by August. He also refused to make a commitment to staying until a final report on his investigation has been completed.
